note: A raised, often elaborate structure supporting a coffin or representing one during funeral ceremonies.
short: A raised structure supporting a coffin.

note: One of the solid upright sections of a battlement, between the gaps.
short: A solid upright section of a battlement.

note: A vessel for burning incense, often suspended on chains.
A fine-grained form of silica, often translucent; varieties include agate and carnelian.
Flashing or sparkling with light.
A monstrous adversary of Zeus in Greek mythology, also called Typhoeus. Hesiod describes him as a son of Earth and Tartarus with a hundred serpent heads. Zeus defeats him with thunderbolts.
short: A many-headed monster opposed to Zeus.

note: A self-moving mechanism or artificial figure. Automata is the Greek-derived plural.
short: A self-moving mechanism or artificial figure.

note: A small room or sleeping chamber; cubicula is the Latin plural.
short: A small room or sleeping chamber.

note: An ancient measure based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
short: An old measure based on the forearm.

note: A spar projecting forward from a ship’s bow, supporting its forward sails and rigging.
short: A spar projecting from a ship’s bow.

note: An extensive, treeless grassy plain of South America.
A communal dining hall, especially in a monastery or religious house.
A candidate seeking admission to a religious order, before becoming a novice.
short: An applicant for admission to a religious order.

note: A rope used to hoist or lower a sail, flag, or spar.
short: A rope used to raise a sail or flag.

note: A long, low couch, often without a back or arms.
short: A low couch or cushioned seat.

note: A staff carried as an emblem of office, especially a bishop’s pastoral staff.
Showy but worthless finery; things that look impressive without having real value.
short: Worthless showy objects or empty nonsense.

note: Formed from small pieces fitted together, like a mosaic or tiled surface.
short: Formed into a mosaic or tiled pattern.

note: Golden in color or ornamented with gold.
In a low, quiet voice.
short: In a quiet or lowered voice.

note: A small writing desk with drawers or compartments for papers.
To flash, sparkle, or give off small bursts of light.
A metal headband that rises broadest above the forehead and narrows toward the temples, worn in ancient Greece.
Greek manteion: an oracle, or the sanctuary where a diviner gives an oracular response. The word belongs to the family of mantis, a seer.

short: A wrestling school or exercise court.
note: A palaestra was a place for wrestling and athletic training in ancient Greece or Rome. The Latin word comes from Greek palaistra, related to palē, wrestling. By extension the word can name a school or place of instruction.

A title used for priests in the story. Compare modern Greek patera, the form used in addressing a father, and pateras, also used for a priest. This is a linguistic comparison, not evidence that the characters are speaking modern Greek.

A title used for the women serving the manteion. Compare Greek mētēra/mitera, mother. Maytera is the book’s spelling, not a standard transliteration; the resemblance should not be treated as a fully documented derivation.
A diviner, especially an official religious interpreter of signs in ancient Rome. Augury sought indications of divine approval or disapproval before an undertaking.

short: A woman credited with prophetic powers.
note: A prophetess through whom a god was believed to speak. Ancient traditions placed sibyls in several regions, including Greece and Italy; the Cumaean Sibyl was especially celebrated.
The public treasury or the revenues belonging to a sovereign. Latin fiscus originally meant a basket and came to designate the imperial treasury.

short: A weapon here; an old alchemical word.
note: In this story, an azoth is a weapon, not a quantity of mercury. Historically azoth names alchemical mercury or a universal remedy. The historical senses explain the borrowed word, not the fictional device’s mechanism.
A monastery or convent where members live in community, rather than as solitary hermits. The name ultimately combines Greek words for common and life.

short: An assistant, especially to a bishop.
note: A helper or colleague in an office. In church usage, a coadjutor assists a bishop and may hold the right to succeed that bishop.
A person appointed to speak for others, or to preside over an assembly. In ecclesiastical usage the title belongs to the chair of a convocation.
The chief clerk of certain courts or other official bodies. The title derives from words meaning first and notary.

short: A basin for washing the hands.
note: A washbasin, especially one supplied from a small tank or vessel above it. Its Latin name means “I shall wash.”
Bronze or brass given a gold surface and used for decorative objects, furniture mounts, and fittings. The French expression or moulu literally means ground gold.

short: An alloy used for strong permanent magnets.
note: An iron-based magnetic alloy containing aluminum and nickel, with cobalt and sometimes other additions. Its name compresses aluminum, nickel, and cobalt.
In Latin, tessera can mean a military watchword as well as the token or tablet used to communicate or authenticate it.
Pas is the masculine singular of the Greek word for all or whole. Its corresponding feminine and neuter forms are pasa and pan.
Hierax is an ancient Greek word for a hawk or falcon. Its stem hierak- appears in compounds and related names.

short: A many-headed sea monster of Greek myth.
note: A monster inhabiting the rocks opposite Charybdis. In Homer’s Odyssey she has six heads on long necks and snatches sailors from vessels passing her cave.
Tartarus, the deep pit below the realm of the dead in Greek cosmology, also personified as a primordial being. In Hesiod the defeated Titans are confined there.
Molpe is one of the Sirens named in the Hesiodic tradition. The Sirens’ alluring song draws passing sailors toward destruction. Her Greek name means song.

short: One of the Sirens of Greek tradition.
note: A Siren named in the account attributed to Apollodorus. The Sirens are supernatural singers whose voices enchant those who hear them.
A form of the Greek name for the sphinx: a creature with a lion’s body, a woman’s head, and wings. The Theban sphinx destroyed travelers who could not answer her riddle, until Oedipus solved it.

short: A powerful machine; a mythic echo.
note: In the story, a talus is a large, powerful machine. The name recalls Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete in Greek myth, but the story’s machine should not be confused with that mythological individual. Ordinary English talus also has anatomical and geological meanings.
Irish sciathán means a wing; it can also denote a projecting side or extension. Its ending is diminutive.
Iolar is the Irish word for an eagle. More specific names combine it with another word, as in iolar mara, a sea eagle.
Grian is the Irish word for the sun. Its genitive form is gréine, found in expressions describing sunlight or solar things.
Irish dreoilín means a wren; dreoilín donn names the Eurasian wren. The word is also found in the Irish name for Wren Day.

short: A shrub with long, red flower tassels.
note: The chenille plant, Acalypha hispida, bears hanging, densely packed tassels of tiny flowers. Their soft, furry appearance gives it the name red-hot cat’s tail. Chenille also names a fuzzy yarn or fabric, from French for caterpillar. The botanical gloss does not exhaust the word’s meanings.

short: A Saharan antelope with spiral horns.
note: A pale-coated desert antelope, Addax nasomaculatus, with long, twisted horns. It is native to the Sahara.
A short-necked seabird of the family Alcidae, typically black and white. Auks use their wings underwater while diving; the extinct great auk, unlike living auks, was flightless.
A babirusa, a wild pig of the genus Babyrousa found in Indonesia. Its name comes from Malay words for pig and deer.
A goatlike mountain mammal, Pseudois nayaur, with a gray-blue coat. It inhabits high country in the Himalayas and neighboring parts of Asia.
A member of the rodent family Caviidae, which includes the guinea pigs. Cavies are not rabbits; the name commonly denotes the short-tailed, rough-haired forms.

short: A large, semiaquatic South American rodent.
note: Also called nutria, the coypu has coarse fur and spends much of its time in and around fresh water. Its scientific name is Myocastor coypus.

A galago, or bushbaby, is a small African primate active chiefly at night and at home in trees. Galagos have large eyes and belong to the family Galagidae. The name is used both broadly and as a zoological genus name.
Theropithecus gelada, a large, long-haired monkey resembling a baboon. It is native to Ethiopia and feeds chiefly on grasses.
A member of Naemorhedus, a genus of mountain-dwelling bovids ranging from the Himalayan region into China. Gorals combine a goatlike build with antelope-like features.

short: A South American relative of the weasels.
note: A low-slung carnivorous mammal with a gray upper coat and darker underparts. Grisons belong to the weasel family; the name comes from French gris, gray.

short: A small, thickset African or Middle Eastern mammal.
note: A short-legged mammal with small ears, a rudimentary tail, and padded feet with broad nails. Hyraxes are also called dassies or coneys.

short: The anvil-shaped bone of the middle ear.
note: The middle one of the three auditory ossicles, between the malleus and stapes. Its Latin name means anvil, describing its shape.
A forest bird with iridescent green upperparts and red underparts. In the resplendent quetzal, the male’s exceptionally long upper tail-coverts extend well beyond the tail itself.

short: A fish with a suction disk on its head.
note: A suckerfish that attaches itself to larger marine animals or other surfaces. The Latin name means delay, from an ancient belief that these fish could hold back a ship.
A tailless or short-tailed, tree-dwelling primate native to southern Asia. Lorises have large eyes and move deliberately along branches.
A woolly-coated primate of tropical Africa, with a short tail and a reduced index finger. Pottos move slowly and grip branches firmly.

short: A small, very large-eyed nocturnal primate.
note: A primate of Southeast Asian islands with long hind limbs and a slender tail. Its conspicuously large eyes suit its nocturnal life.
A small nocturnal rodent of arid parts of Africa and Asia. Its elongated hind legs and long balancing tail support rapid, kangaroo-like leaps.

short: A coarse, naturally brownish wild silk.
note: Silk produced by certain moths other than the domesticated mulberry silkworm. The word, from Hindi and Urdu tasar, also names the moth or caterpillar producing it.

short: A slender, spotted or banded forest mammal.
note: A small, long-tailed carnivore of tropical forests. The name applies to Asian Prionodon and African Poiana, animals resembling civets.
A nocturnal rodent of tropical America, with a stocky body and rows of pale spots along its flanks.
Aplodontia rufa, a burrowing rodent of western North America. Mountain beaver is another name for this animal.
A mustelid with conspicuous black-and-white markings and strong-smelling defensive secretions. The name is also written zorille.
Mellivora capensis, a tough-bodied member of the weasel family found in Africa and parts of Asia. Its upper coat is pale and its underside dark.
Gulo is the zoological genus containing the wolverine. The Latin word gulo means a glutton.
Xiphias is the genus of the common swordfish. The Greek name is related to xiphos, a sword.

short: A fly of the blackfly family.
note: A member of the family Simuliidae, the small flies commonly called blackflies. The word comes from the genus Simulium.
A parasitic flatworm of the class Trematoda. Many flukes have a flattened body and suckers by which they attach to their hosts.
An Anglo-Indian word for a camel, borrowed from Hindi and Urdu. It is also encountered in Australian usage.

short: The aurochs, an extinct wild ox.
note: An old name for the aurochs, the wild ancestor of domestic cattle. Urus was the Latin name for this animal.
The preliminary study of a text’s literary and historical background, especially study preparing for the interpretation of the Bible.
Related to hierology: religious lore and literature, or the study of sacred things.
Hylotelephium telephium, formerly Sedum telephium, is a perennial succulent with clusters of small, star-shaped pink or purplish flowers. It is also called live-forever.
Daphne mezereum bears fragrant rose-purple flowers before its leaves and later produces bright berries. The plant is poisonous.
The Hebrew noun orev means a raven or crow. The older transliteration Oreb preserves a b for the same Hebrew consonant.
Kypris, also written Cypris, is a name of Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty.

short: A half-woman, half-serpent of Greek myth.
note: In Hesiod’s Theogony, Echidna has a nymph’s upper body and an immense snake’s lower body. With Typhon she is the mother of monsters including Cerberus and the Hydra.

short: A person taught by a god.
note: Greek theodidaktos means taught by God, combining theos, god, with didaktos, taught. The adjective appears in 1 Thessalonians 4:9.

short: A visible appearance of a deity.
note: A manifestation in which a god becomes visible. The word comes through Greek theophaneia, combining the divine with the idea of appearing.
The governing council of a town or city, consisting of its mayor and councillors.
A court or judicial office; also the place where the judge exercises that office.
The edge of a body of water: the shore of the sea, or the bank of a river or lake.
Spanish alameda originally denotes a grove of poplars; it also names a public walk planted with trees.

short: A bristly-headed plant used in cloth finishing.
note: A plant of the genus Dipsacus. The dried heads of fuller’s teasel have hooked prickles and were used to raise a nap on woven cloth.
Mucor comprises molds that produce spores in rounded or cylindrical spore cases. The Latin name means mold.
Scleroderma is a genus of tough-skinned, puffball-like fungi. Their interior darkens as the spores mature; the fungi form close associations with tree roots.
Anthriscus cerefolium, an aromatic herb of the carrot family. Its divided leaves are used in salads, soups, and other dishes.
A chiefly southern African genus of fleshy-leaved plants. Its name comes from Latin crassus, thick; older botanical usage included certain stonecrops.
A member of a group of green algae whose cells are often joined or divided into matching halves. The name derives from Greek desmos, a bond.
In a subtraction, the subtrahend is the quantity taken away. In 9 minus 4, it is 4; the starting quantity is the minuend.
Also called a jupon: a shirtlike garment, often padded or quilted, worn beneath armor. The word is related to French jupe.

short: A keyboard instrument with wheel-bowed strings.
note: A harpsichord-shaped instrument whose strings sound through contact with revolving wheels, rather than by plucking.

short: A glossy black, red-legged crow relative.
note: A bird of the genus Pyrrhocorax, with dark, glossy plumage and red legs. The English name is pronounced “chuff.”
Palustria is a neuter plural form of the Latin adjective paluster, marshy or swampy. It belongs to the same word family as palus, a marsh.
Amnis names flowing water, especially a river or a strong current. Its Latin plural is amnes.
A city or walled town. In Roman usage, urbs without further qualification can mean Rome itself.
Ancient Greek hus, written ὗς, means a pig or hog. The noun can be used of either sex.

short: An earthy deposit rich in lime.
note: Loose or crumbly sediment containing a substantial amount of calcium carbonate, mixed with materials such as clay, sand, or silt.

short: A metal used to strengthen steel.
note: A metallic element, symbol Mo, added to steel for strength and hardness. Its name descends from Greek molybdos, lead.
A large genus of herbs and shrubs in the mint family, including culinary sage and many flowering garden plants. The Latin name means sage.
Old cant for the chief of a group of thieves or vagrants. It combines the approving dimber, “fine,” with damber; historical dictionaries also print it as two words or a hyphenated compound.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: An old cant word for a dog, recorded in Francis Grose’s dictionary of slang.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: Food carried or obtained for a meal. As a verb, prog also means to forage.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: An old slang term for money. Historical dictionaries also spell it lowr.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: A cant term for a man. A bob cull is a good-natured fellow.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: An old cant term for a woman, as recorded in Grose’s historical slang dictionary.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A low sighing or moaning sound.
note: A low, continuous sighing, rushing, or moaning sound, especially the sound of wind among trees or through a narrow opening. The verb means to make that sound.
Playing lightly over a surface, as a small flame does; by extension, softly glowing or radiant. The underlying Latin verb means to lick, an image of flame touching a surface without consuming it.
Dry, withered, or stripped of freshness, especially of vegetation. A literary description of leaves or land, rather than a statement about temperature alone.
Possibly Old French viron, a circle or the country round about. It belongs to the family of virer, “to turn,” and environ, “around.”

short: Possibly Termagant, a medieval stage deity.
note: Possibly Termagant, an imaginary deity of medieval European literature. Christian writers wrongly ascribed this figure to Muslims; on the stage the character became a noisy, overbearing tyrant. The later English insult termagant developed from that theatrical tradition.
Spanish alambrera is wire mesh or a protective wire cover, such as a screen over a window or food. It is formed from alambre, wire; the central image is an enclosing barrier.
An oosik is the baculum, or penile bone, of a walrus. The word comes from Iñupiaq usuk. It names a particular anatomical structure, not the animal as a whole.
Irish aer means air, the atmosphere, or the open air. It is the ordinary language word rather than the name of a particular bird.
Irish mear means quick, nimble, or lively. It can also mean hasty or rash: speed in action can become haste in judgment.
Irish canna means a can or container. This noun should be distinguished from the Scottish and northern English contraction canna, “cannot.”

short: A small shrine or framed niche.
note: A small shrine or a niche given the architectural form of a little building. The name comes from Latin aedicula, a diminutive of aedes, a house or temple.

short: Latin: a bath or bathing room.
note: Latin balneum means a bath, bathing place, or bathing room. The word was borrowed from Greek balaneion and is the ancestor of English terms beginning balneo-, concerned with baths.
A little dining room. Latin cenatiuncula is a diminutive of cenatio, a room for dining; the diminutive makes the room small or intimate rather than a large banqueting hall.

short: Latin: a school or place of study.
note: Latin schola means a school, lecture, or learned discussion. It comes from Greek scholē, leisure devoted to study: the word’s history links learning with time free from other work.
A strong distilled spirit, related to Portuguese aguardente and Spanish aguardiente. Both names literally describe “burning water”; the word does not specify a single ingredient or fixed strength.

Possibly formed from Greek chrēsmos, an oracle or prophetic response, with a suffix concerned with speech or discourse. “Oracular writings” is therefore a plausible reading; the exact formation remains uncertain.
Old cant for pretty or fine; “dimber hands” can accordingly mean fine or capable hands.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: A dark lantern used in housebreaking, its light concealed when necessary.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: An old abbreviation of diligence, a stagecoach; also used for a post-chaise.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: An insulting word for a bulky woman.
note: An old derogatory term for a fat, awkward, or lazy woman.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: Slang for eyes, also written glimms. A singular glim can instead mean a candle or lantern.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: An old spelling of foist: to insert secretly or fraudulently, especially with “in.”

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: A cant expression meaning too much, rather than a particular denomination of money.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

note: Cant for speaking civilly or ingratiatingly; also recorded as “cut bene whiddes.”

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: An Asian vine with aromatic leaves.
note: Betel is the climbing pepper vine Piper betle, whose leaves are chewed with areca nut. The leaf and the so-called betel nut come from different plants.

short: A flowering plant of the pink family.
note: Campion is a common name for several flowering plants of the pink family, traditionally assigned to Lychnis and Silene. The name does not select one particular species.

short: A plant of the genus Polygala.
note: Milkworts are plants of the genus Polygala. The traditional name reflects an old belief that such plants increased milk production; the name is not a promise of that effect.
A name related to asphodel, a flowering plant of the genus Asphodelus. The Greek-derived name is used for plants with tall flower spikes and lily-like blossoms.
Possibly martagon, the lily whose petals curl strongly backward in a turban-like shape. The usual botanical spelling is martagon; the personal name is left unchanged.

short: A stand or frame for a coffin.
note: A frame or stand on which a dead body or coffin is carried or displayed. The word is related to bear in the sense of carrying a weight.

short: A railing supported by small pillars.
note: A row of small pillars, called balusters, supporting a rail. The term names the whole barrier along a stair, balcony, or terrace, rather than one of its supports.
The ceremonies performed for someone who has died. The word is normally plural and concerns the observances surrounding burial, rather than the grave itself.
A woolen or cotton cloth with a felt-like surface. It is commonly used to cover gaming tables and to line or cover doors, where its thickness helps soften noise.

short: Silkworm fiber; also a personal name.
note: Silk is the fine fiber spun by silkworms and used to make cloth. It is an animal product, not itself an animal. The word also has botanical uses, including the threadlike parts of an ear of corn; those meanings do not establish a hidden identity for the character.

short: An animal’s horn; also a personal name.
note: An animal’s projecting horn, or the hard material from which it is formed. A cattle horn has a bony core covered with keratin. The name belongs to the vocabulary of animal parts and products, not just animal species.

In anatomy, a villus is a small projecting structure, notably one of the fingerlike projections lining the small intestine. The Latin word originally referred to shaggy hair. Here it is used as a personal name.

Nettles, especially plants of the genus Urtica, bear hairs that can sting the skin. The verb nettle means to irritate or provoke; that ordinary sense is distinct from identifying the character’s role.

The familiar garden hyacinth, Hyacinthus orientalis, grows from a bulb and carries clusters of scented flowers. The ancient plant name had a less certain botanical reference; the word has also been used for gemstones. The flower meaning is relevant to the plant-name pattern here.

Marble is limestone altered by heat and pressure into crystalline rock, widely used for sculpture and buildings. The personal name draws on a material word; it does not mean that the character is literally made of marble.

Pike names a long-bodied freshwater fish with conspicuous teeth. The same English spelling also denotes a long thrusting weapon. The fish sense fits the animal vocabulary of these personal names; a weapon-only gloss would miss it.

short: An animal scent used in perfumery.
note: Musk originally denotes a strongly scented secretion obtained from the male musk deer. It also names similar scents and their substitutes. As a personal name it can therefore refer to an animal product, rather than to a species.
Mint names aromatic herbs, especially of the genus Mentha. This botanical meaning fits the personal name; the unrelated word for a place that makes coins is a different sense.

short: A flowering shrub; a plant name.
note: A rose is a shrub of the genus Rosa, or its flower. The plant word is used here as a personal name. Its presence does not identify the character with a particular rose species or establish a particular religious symbol.
Sinew is an old word for a tendon, the tough tissue joining muscle to bone. It also suggests bodily strength. As a name, it belongs with words for animal parts and materials.

short: A song or expression of praise.
note: A celebratory song of praise or thanksgiving; by extension, an enthusiastic tribute. The word comes from Greek hymns associated with Apollo.
Looking worn down, exhausted, or damaged, especially in the face. It describes an appearance rather than a particular illness.
Lake Limna is a named lake in the story. Possibly the name echoes Greek limnē, a lake or pool. The Greek meaning is documented; its use as Wolfe’s intended derivation remains an inference.

The title of Viron’s civic ruler. Possibly related to Spanish alcalde, a mayor or chief municipal magistrate, ultimately from Arabic al-qāḍī, the judge. That comparison explains a likely linguistic background, not identical powers or institutions.

short: A world; also a spiral or ring.
note: In these books, whorl is used for a world. In ordinary English it means a spiral, coil, or arrangement of parts around an axis. The fictional use and the dictionary meaning are distinct; the note does not explain the world’s hidden history.

short: A building material in the story.
note: The story’s name for a hard building material, used in blocks and walls. This is a contextual gloss: no specific chemical composition or real geological rock is implied.
Inhumi is the plural form; one is an inhumu. These are beings of the fictional setting. This note identifies the word forms without revealing their origins, abilities, or individual identities.
